title: Answering Questions from the Access Log
intro: The access log has one line per request: who asked, for what, what they got, and how long it took. With awk, sort, and uniq it answers most incident questions in seconds, before any dashboard loads. You're in /var/log/nginx on web-1. In the default 'combined' format, field 1 is the client address, field 7 the path, and field 9 the status code. This server's format adds the request time as the last field.

steps.prompt: Errors are being reported. Count the requests in access.log by status code, most frequent first.
expected_commands: awk '{print $9}' access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn
awk '{print $9}' access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -nr
awk '{ print $9 }' access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn
steps.why: This is the first cut in almost any web incident: how bad, and what kind. 'sort | uniq -c | sort -rn' is the counting idiom to know by heart; uniq only merges adjacent lines, which is why the first sort is needed. 502 points at the upstream application. 499 isn't a server error at all: it's nginx recording that the client hung up before the answer was ready, usually because the answer was slow.

steps.prompt: Which paths are returning those errors? Show the top paths among responses with a status of 500 or above.
expected_commands: awk '$9 >= 500 {print $7}' access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head
awk '$9 >= 500 {print $7}' access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -nr | head
awk '$9 >= 500 { print $7 }' access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head
awk '$9 >= 500 {print $7}' access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -10
steps.hint: awk '$9 >= 500 {print $7}' access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head
steps.explanation: Nearly all of them are one endpoint: /api/checkout.
steps.why: A condition before the braces makes awk print only matching lines, so this is a filter and a projection in one step. Knowing it's one endpoint, not the whole site, changes the diagnosis: not 'the app is down' but 'something checkout depends on is failing'.

steps.prompt: Is one client responsible for a lot of the traffic? Show the 5 busiest client addresses.
expected_commands: awk '{print $1}' access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -5
awk '{print $1}' access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -nr | head -5
awk '{print $1}' access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -n 5
awk '{ print $1 }' access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -5
steps.explanation: One address made 61,204 requests, fifty times more than anyone else.
steps.why: A single address far above the rest is a scraper, a broken client retrying in a loop, or an attack. Check before blocking: it could be a partner's server, a corporate network behind one address, or your own load balancer if the real client address isn't being restored (webservers-incident-006).

steps.prompt: See what that client is asking for: show the top paths requested by 203.0.113.77.
expected_commands: grep '^203.0.113.77 ' access.log | awk '{print $7}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head
grep "^203.0.113.77 " access.log | awk '{print $7}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head
grep 203.0.113.77 access.log | awk '{print $7}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head
awk '$1 == "203.0.113.77" {print $7}' access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head
steps.explanation: It's hammering /api/checkout: the same endpoint that's failing.
steps.why: Two findings just joined up: one client is flooding checkout, and checkout is where the 502s are. Whether it's a cause or a symptom (a client retrying because checkout fails) needs the timeline, which is why you look at when each started. Either way the next tutorials' tools apply: a rate limit to contain it, and the error log to see why the upstream fails.

steps.prompt: Find the slowest requests. The request time in seconds is the last field: print it with the path, sorted so the slowest come first, top 5.
expected_commands: awk '{print $NF, $7}' access.log | sort -rn | head -5
awk '{print $NF, $7}' access.log | sort -nr | head -5
awk '{print $NF, $7}' access.log | sort -rn | head -n 5
awk '{ print $NF, $7 }' access.log | sort -rn | head -5
steps.explanation: Report exports take exactly 60 seconds, which is a timeout, not a duration.
steps.why: $NF is awk's last field. A cluster of times at a round number is a limit being hit: 60.00 is proxy_read_timeout's default. The default log format doesn't record timing at all, so add $request_time and $upstream_response_time to log_format on every server. The first is the total as the client saw it; the second is the app's share. A large gap between them is a slow client or a slow network, not a slow app.

steps.prompt: Watch the errors as they happen: follow error.log.
expected_commands: tail -f error.log
sudo tail -f error.log
tail -f /var/log/nginx/error.log
sudo tail -f /var/log/nginx/error.log
steps.fake_output: 2026/09/28 11:40:07 [error] 88120#88120: *914402 connect() failed (111: Connection refused) while connecting to upstream, client: 203.0.113.77, server: shop.example.com, request: "POST /api/checkout HTTP/1.1", upstream: "http://10.0.1.12:8080/api/checkout", host: "shop.example.com"
steps.explanation: The reason behind a 502: nginx tried 10.0.1.12:8080 and the connection was refused.
steps.why: The access log says what happened; the error log says why. Every 502, 503, and 504 that nginx generates has a line here naming the upstream it tried and the system error it got. The next tutorial is about reading those lines.
